Recognising the collective systems of care that are working to support and strengthen breastfeeding this World Breastfeeding Week, as the ANMF works to protect, support and advocate for a positive breastfeeding culture.

Healthy, economical and sustainable - the benefits of breastfeeding are known, and its success relies on a warm chain of support and collective systems of care. 

This includes access to timely and appropriate breastfeeding support, workplace protections, and supportive social networks, rather than expecting individual mothers to carry the responsibility alone.

Let’s strengthen what works.

The country’s largest union, the ANMF, has paid tribute to the work of ACTU Secretary Sally McManus and President Michele O’Neil, who have announced they are leaving the organisation.

ANMF Federal Secretary Annie Butler, who also sits as ACTU Vice President, said Sally and Michele made an extraordinary collective contribution to the nation’s industrial relations (IR) system, delivering a raft of reforms that improved the everyday lives of Australian workers.

Media Release: https://bit.ly/44Ut0QJ

New data showing the number of healthcare workers hospitalised after being assaulted at work has more than doubled in a decade confirms years of warnings about worsening safety of healthcare workers, say the Australian College of Nursing (ACN) and the Australian Nursing and Midwifery Federation (ANMF).

National figures released by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare show assault has now climbed from the fourth to the second leading cause of hospitalisation for injuries among healthcare workers. By comparison, assault ranks seventh for the general Australian population.

“This should not be a wake-up call, because nurses and their colleagues have been sounding the alarm about this for years,” said ACN Chief Executive Officer, Adjunct Professor Kathryn Zeitz FACN. “But this data definitively shows that there can be no more excuses for inaction.”

“Nurses, midwives and personal care workers continue to be attacked, abused and intimidated in their workplaces. We also know that workplace violence and aggression (WVA) is underreported, so the true scale of the problem could be much worse,” ANMF Federal Secretary Annie Butler explained.

“Urgent action, including improved staffing levels, and additional security measures, is needed, so nurses, midwives and personal care workers are safe on the job. There must be zero tolerance for any form of WVA against frontline health workers,” said Ms Butler.

The ANMF has expressed serious concerns with the joint statement recently released by Ahpra on eliminating antisemitism in healthcare, in particular its adoption of the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition of antisemitism. 
The ANMF strongly opposes antisemitism and all forms of racial or religious discrimination in the provision of healthcare and has called on the Board and Ahpra to take action, including immediately suspending the endorsement and application of the IHRA definition. 
Full statement: https://bit.ly/4w66hwX

The ANMF has welcomed new landmark Legislation that now gives patients access to subsidised Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) medicines prescribed by registered nurses.

The passing of the Health Legislation Amendment (Prescribing of Pharmaceutical Benefits) Bill 2025 in Federal Parliament today marks another significant step forward in allowing highly qualified registered nurses to work to their full scope of practice.

The Legislation allows designated registered nurses (RNs) to prescribe medicines under the PBS, ensuring patients pay the same subsidised price for nurse‑prescribed medicines as they do for those prescribed by a doctor.

Nurses and midwives are the solution. 

At Federal Parliament, ANMF Federal Secretary Annie Butler and Federal Assistant Secretary Catelyn Richards joined nursing and midwifery organisations, showing parliamentarians first-hand what nurses and midwives can deliver in the primary care sector with innovative, evidence-based, person-centred nurse- and midwife-led solutions. 

From nurse-led skin-cancer checks and wound closure to rural and remote-area advanced care, and maternity care for both mothers and babies, the Parliamentary Friends of Nursing event in the Mural Hall, highlights the growing role of nurses and midwives in delivering timely, effective health care across the community, enabling people to access high-quality care, when and where they need it.

At the helm of Western Australia’s largest union, Australian Nursing and Midwifery Federation WA, Romina Raschilla now leads a sweeping rebuild focused on getting back to what matters most to members.

A first-generation Australian with Italian parents and three adult children, Ms Raschilla began her professional life outside healthcare, working in the corporate sector. It was after the birth of her third child that she made a decisive change, enrolling in a Bachelor of Science (Nursing) with the aim of becoming a midwife.

“I always wanted to work with families and once I started doing neonatal and paediatric shifts, I realised that was giving me the opportunity I was looking for - to care not only for the patient but also for their parents.”

Her nursing career took her across a broad range of specialties, including paediatrics, orthopaedics and cardiothoracic care, in both public and private hospitals. She later moved into regional and remote health, worked as an aged care facility manager, and completed an MBA in human resources management. 

Ms Raschilla’s entry into union leadership in 2022 came from a strong desire to engage with members and ensure full advocacy on their behalf.

Since then, the union has undergone rapid reform.

Governance and communication systems have been rebuilt, with members now making about 800 direct calls each month to seek industrial advice.

A key priority has been updating the union’s name to include the state’s valued midwives and to replace ‘Perth’ with ‘WA’ to better reflect its diverse membership base.

A formal delegate and organiser structure — standard across unions nationally — is being rolled out.

“Members are learning what it means to be delegates, to organise, to advocate,” said Ms Raschilla. “And they’re excited.”

For Ms Raschilla, the work has been “like building a plane while flying it”, but the energy from members and delegates makes it worthwhile.

“Our nurses, midwives and carers are incredibly resilient, but they’re tired,” she said. “They deserve a union that fights hard for them, so they can keep caring for the community safely and sustainably.”

The ANMF will join nursing and midwifery leaders from across the country at Parliament House today for a ‘hands-on’ demonstration of the high-quality, clinical capabilities of Australia's largest health workforce.

The Parliamentary Friends of Nursing event in the Mural Hall, will highlight the growing role of nurses and midwives in delivering timely, effective health care across the community, enabling people to access high-quality care, when and where they need it.

ANMF Federal Secretary Annie Butler said the event will showcase nurse- and midwife-led models of care and the impact they can have on health outcomes when nurses and midwives work to their full scope of practice.

Health researchers are calling for urgent action to better support graduate nurses, with emotional burnout in the first year of practice a key driver of early workforce attrition in the sector. 

Unsupportive workplaces, role stress and unrealistic workload expectations were identified as the three dominant factors contributing to burnout among newly qualified registered nurses (RNs) in a scoping review conducted by James Cook University (JCU).
